name: e04_walk_forward
title: 4. Walk-forward: does re-optimising the windows beat a fixed textbook rule?
text:
**Question.** Does re-optimising the EMA windows every year on the past 5 years beat simply fixing 50/200 in advance, on dates neither has seen?

**Setup.** Rolling walk-forward over the 62-pair grid: each fold picks the best-Sharpe pair on 5 years, then trades it for 1 year, with a one-bar embargo and switching costs at the fold boundary. The static 50/200 and buy-and-hold are measured over exactly the same OOS dates; triples below are Sharpe / CAGR / MaxDD.

**Findings.**

- SPY (2001-2026, 25 folds): WF 0.57 / 8.6% / -34%, 50/200 0.53 / 8.3% / -36%, B&H 0.53 / 10.4% / -55%.
- QQQ (2007-2026, 19 folds): WF 0.71 / 12.9% / -29%, 50/200 0.81 / 15.7% / -29%, B&H 0.72 / 16.3% / -51%.
- BTC (2022-2026, 5 folds): WF 0.50 / 16.6% / -40%, 50/200 0.89 / 35.3% / -28%, B&H 0.40 / 12.6% / -67%.
- GLD (2013-2026, 13 folds): WF 0.47 / 7.5% / -23%, 50/200 0.36 / 6.0% / -31%, B&H 0.48 / 8.6% / -27%.
- Walk-forward beats the fixed rule on 2 of 4 assets (SPY, GLD) and trails on QQQ, BTC; the average Sharpe difference is -0.09. No asset shows a significant gain from re-optimising after Holm adjustment across the 8 walk-forward tests (one-sided paired stationary bootstrap; 95% CIs of the gap: SPY -0.16 to +0.23; QQQ -0.28 to +0.08; BTC -1.07 to +0.21; GLD -0.11 to +0.36); it is worse at the uncorrected 5% level on QQQ anchored (one-sided p = 0.017), but not significantly after Holm across the 8 walk-forward tests. An anchored (expanding) training window beats 50/200 on 2 of 4 (SPY, GLD).
- The chosen pair changes at 35 of 58 fold boundaries. Its OOS Sharpe ranks, on average, at the 44%-54% percentile of all 62 candidates in the same test year (50% = a random pick), and it beats 50/200 in 20%-60% of the test years where the two differ. Walk-forward efficiency: SPY 0.74, QQQ 0.83, BTC 0.23, GLD 1.14.

**Interpretation.** Walk-forward analysis (Pardo 2008) removes the look-ahead in the *choice* of parameters, the step the README's Bitcoin re-tuning (12/128, then 50/200) skipped, but it cannot create information that is not there. Experiment 3 showed how little the in-sample ranking of these rules carries out of sample. Here the yearly re-selection lands close to the middle of the candidate pack out of sample while hopping between near-equivalent rules. The out-of-sample edge of optimisation over a rule chosen a priori is negative on average and statistically indistinguishable from zero. This is one reason practitioners fix and diversify lookbacks rather than tune them: Hurst, Ooi & Pedersen (2017) average 1-, 3- and 12-month signals across a century of data. Optimisation is a source of selection bias (Bailey et al. 2017), and the fair benchmark for a tuned rule is the untuned one. If anything the test favours the static rule, whose "a priori" status is partly earned ex post: 50/200 became the textbook rule by working on past US equity data (Sullivan, Timmermann & White 1999). Walk-forward beats buy-and-hold's Sharpe by more than 0.01 on 2 of 4 assets (SPY, BTC), yet earns a lower CAGR on 3 (SPY, QQQ, GLD). Against buy-and-hold, walk-forward trades return for a shallower drawdown (SPY, QQQ, GLD) and out-earns it with a shallower drawdown (BTC); the static rule trades return for a shallower drawdown (SPY, QQQ), out-earns it with a shallower drawdown (BTC) and earns less with a deeper drawdown (GLD). BTC has only 4.6 OOS years (5 folds) after the slow-EMA warm-up and the 5-year training window, so its numbers are anecdotes.
after: Walk-forward efficiency here is the ratio of mean OOS to mean in-sample excess return of the chosen configurations. Values near or above 1 do not mean the optimiser is skilled: when every candidate earns roughly the same trend premium, OOS and IS returns of *whatever* is chosen are similar, so WFE measures the stability of the premium, not the value of choosing.
